historic_survey.note: City Landmark No. 267, and the last of the six religious and fraternal buildings the statement counts. A fanciful blend of the Craftsman and Art Nouveau styles with ornament nominally derived from traditional Swedish architecture, though the statement judges the result more German or Swiss than Swedish. The interior is almost entirely original: lodge rooms, a banqueting hall, a kitchen, a library, club rooms and a bar, with the Café du Nord rathskeller in the basement. Christopher VerPlanck's context statement of 2022 surveyed 552 properties in Duboce Triangle for the Duboce Triangle Neighborhood Association.

historical_record.description: Built under a contract of 4 May 1907 for $35,000 by a consortium of Swedish contractors — Andrew Olson, Carlson & Swanson, and Victor Stanquist — to a design by the Swedish immigrant architect August Nordin, and financed by a $40,000 loan from Eric O. Lindholm, a Swedish immigrant gold miner and banker, whom a contemporary Vestkusten article names as E. Lindblom. One of its two retail spaces was leased to the Swedish-American Mercantile Company, a dealer in imported wines and liquors and a delicatessen selling Scandinavian and German specialties.

hook: Swedish American Hall, City Landmark No. 267 — built by Swedish contractors in 1907 and still the Swedish Society's.
